claims.claim: `telemetry.includeRuntimeContext` marks which top-level runtimeContext properties are sent to telemetry; with `{requestId: true}` telemetry receives only `{requestId}`, and properties set to `false` or omitted are excluded.
claims.explanation: filterIncludedContext keeps only keys whose flag is exactly `false`. The condition is inverted relative to the docs, the type comment and the test. A key set to `true` is dropped, an omitted key is dropped, and a key set to `false` is passed to telemetry. So `{requestId: true}` yields `{}`, and `{secret: false}` sends the secret.
claims.user_impact: A user who writes `includeRuntimeContext: { userId: false }` to keep an identifier out of telemetry sends that identifier to every registered integration. A user who sets `true` on the fields they want gets none of them. The same function filters events for all telemetry integrations.

source.quote: In this example, telemetry integrations receive `runtimeContext` as `{ requestId: 'req_abc' }`. Properties set to `false` or omitted are excluded.

evidence.quote: Runtime context properties are excluded unless they are explicitly set to `true`.

review.reason: The filter keeps only entries whose include flag is === false, so true and omitted keys are dropped and false keys are sent. This is the inverse of the docs. Severity high is fair.

claims.claim: Tool context such as API keys is kept out of telemetry unless selected with `telemetry.includeToolsContext`.
claims.explanation: Tool context uses the same inverted filter. A tool-context key set to `true` is removed, and a key set to `false` is forwarded to telemetry. The default with no `includeToolsContext` is an empty object, which is safe.
claims.user_impact: A user who sets `includeToolsContext: { weather: { weatherApiKey: false } }` to hide the key would send the API key to telemetry providers. Opting fields in with `true` silently removes them.

review.reason: Tool context goes through the same inverted filter (filterToolContext calls filterIncludedContext), so keys set to false are sent and keys set to true are removed.

behaviors.behavior: When no auth environment variable is set, the Claude Code harness reads the user's own Claude Code OAuth credentials from ~/.claude/.credentials.json or the macOS Keychain. It refreshes the token against platform.claude.com and writes the refreshed credentials back to the user's keychain entry or file, then supplies the access token to the agent as CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN.
behaviors.user_impact: Developers who run the harness locally with no API key set have their personal Claude subscription login used, and the stored login is silently rewritten with a rotated refresh token. The access token is also handed to the agent runtime, which can end up in a remote sandbox when that sandbox lacks request-transformation support. The docs say only that the adapter "attempts to resolve a native subscription from the host system"; they don't mention the keychain or credential-file reads, the token refresh, or the write-back.
behaviors.docs_searched: content/providers/02-ai-sdk-harnesses/01-claude-code.mdx (auth section, lines 141-185) and all of content/ for "native subscription", "keychain" and "credentials.json". Only a one-line mention of resolving a native subscription exists, repeated across the harness pages.

review.reason: The code reads the keychain, refreshes the token against platform.claude.com and passes the result as CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN. The docs say only that the adapter resolves a native subscription. Medium severity is fair.

raw_claims.claim: `telemetry.includeRuntimeContext` marks which top-level runtimeContext properties are sent to telemetry; with `{requestId: true}` telemetry receives only `{requestId}`, and properties set to `false` or omitted are excluded.
raw_claims.explanation: filterIncludedContext keeps only keys whose flag is exactly `false`. The condition is inverted relative to the docs, the type comment and the test. A key set to `true` is dropped, an omitted key is dropped, and a key set to `false` is passed to telemetry. So `{requestId: true}` yields `{}`, and `{secret: false}` sends the secret.
raw_claims.user_impact: A user who writes `includeRuntimeContext: { userId: false }` to keep an identifier out of telemetry sends that identifier to every registered integration. A user who sets `true` on the fields they want gets none of them. The same function filters events for all telemetry integrations.

source.quote: In this example, telemetry integrations receive `runtimeContext` as `{ requestId: 'req_abc' }`. Properties set to `false` or omitted are excluded.

evidence.quote: Runtime context properties are excluded unless they are explicitly set to `true`.

review.reason: The filter keeps only entries whose include flag is === false, so true and omitted keys are dropped and false keys are sent. This is the inverse of the docs. Severity high is fair.

raw_claims.claim: Tool context such as API keys is kept out of telemetry unless selected with `telemetry.includeToolsContext`.
raw_claims.explanation: Tool context uses the same inverted filter. A tool-context key set to `true` is removed, and a key set to `false` is forwarded to telemetry. The default with no `includeToolsContext` is an empty object, which is safe.
raw_claims.user_impact: A user who sets `includeToolsContext: { weather: { weatherApiKey: false } }` to hide the key would send the API key to telemetry providers. Opting fields in with `true` silently removes them.

source.quote: Tool-specific context can also contain values that are useful during execution but should not be sent to telemetry providers, such as API keys or access tokens.

evidence.quote: Tool context properties are excluded unless they are explicitly set to `true`.

review.reason: Tool context goes through the same inverted filter (filterToolContext calls filterIncludedContext), so keys set to false are sent and keys set to true are removed.

raw_claims.claim: Telemetry is opt-out: passing `telemetry: { isEnabled: false }` disables telemetry events for that call, including tracing-channel events.
raw_claims.explanation: The early return that builds the no-op dispatcher fires on `isEnabled === true`, not `false`, which contradicts the comment above it, the docs and the unit tests. With `isEnabled: false` the normal dispatcher is built and all registered or per-call integrations still receive events. `isEnabled: true` is what silences telemetry. Nothing else in the package reads `isEnabled`, so there is no other opt-out switch. The only stream-text path that checks `isEnabled !== false` does not stop the dispatcher.
raw_claims.user_impact: A user who sets `isEnabled: false` on a call carrying sensitive prompts, expecting it to stay out of OpenTelemetry or other registered integrations, still has inputs and outputs sent. The explicit per-call opt-out does not work.

raw_claims.claim: OpenAI compaction items are returned as text parts with special providerMetadata and sent back as compaction input items on later requests.
raw_claims.explanation: The round trip works, but the returned parts have type `custom` and kind `openai.compaction`, not `text`. On the way back, the converter sends an item reference when `store` is on, skips the item when a conversation is used, and sends the encrypted compaction item otherwise.
raw_claims.user_impact: A user who persists only parts with type `text` (as the docs imply they can recognise compaction items) drops the compaction state, which breaks the carried-forward context on the next turn.

source.quote: compaction items are returned as text parts with special `providerMetadata`, and when passed back in subsequent requests they are sent as compaction input items.

review.reason: The code emits the compaction item as a part of type 'custom' with kind 'openai.compaction', not as a text part as the docs say. Persisting only text parts would lose it. Low severity fits.
